speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will address my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the findings of the National Energy Board that the export levels for light crude oil should be phased out by 1980-81, that our own crude oil will no longer be sufficient to meet our requirements between 1981 and 1983 and that we will need net imports of 450,000 barrels a day by 1985, that lack of action on the tar sands project means that the next tar sands plant will not come on stream until 1987 and in light of the lack of effective steps being taken for conservation through developing the tar sands, solar energy or hydro energy, will the minister tell the House when the government will adopt and implement effective energy policies and how they plan to meet this grim prospect outlined in the latest National Energy Board report? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources relates to the National Energy Board's prediction which seems to be based largely on this government's past performance in energy, that by 1985 this country will be importing nearly half a million barrels of oil per day. In view of the highly authoritative report from the workshop on alternative energy sources which suggests that there may be a world shortage of oil by 1985, will the minister tell the House what he plans to do if the half million daily barrels of imports are not available by 1985 and is his alternative to ration oil supplies for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINGENCY PLANS IF IMPORTED OIL NOT AVAILABLE-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF NEXT TAR SANDS PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would refer to the "Energy Strategy for Canada, Policies for Self-Reliance" published one year ago, he would see that we fully anticipated these sorts of difficulties. Indeed, we set up a number of responses for increasing supplies. The hon. member may know that for many months we have tried to negotiate a different set of fiscal terms, to provide incentive for the development of the

yet underdeveloped leases of the tar sands and the heavy oils of Alberta. I believe it will be possible to produce close to a million barrels a day of oil and heavy oil from the tar sands by 1990.

subtopic: CONTINGENCY PLANS IF IMPORTED OIL NOT AVAILABLE-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF NEXT TAR SANDS PROJECT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Since, according to the predictions of the National Energy Board, continued delays will slow down the development of the heavy oil sands in Alberta, may I ask the minister how quickly he expects the next development plan to be implemented and what is being negotiated at present to ensure that by 1985, not 1990, we will have another oil development project in the tar sands?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINGENCY PLANS IF IMPORTED OIL NOT AVAILABLE-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF NEXT TAR SANDS PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the chances are pretty good. Indeed, the energy minister of Alberta said, after the energy ministers meeting three weeks ago at which we discussed what the price of oil for Canada should be, that, given the scenario the majority of energy ministers accepted, Alberta would be prepared to develop aggressively-I think that was his phrase-the tar sands and heavy oils of Alberta. If we can secure the co-operation of the province of Alberta in this national task and reach the one million barrels a day production to which I referred, instead of the close to 500,000 barrels a day the National Energy Board set out in its report, we shall approach the target we set.
My figures indicate that we should be able to reduce our dependence on foreign oil to a lesser figure than we mentioned in the Energy Strategy one year ago. That will require considerable effort on the conservation side. It will require the implementation of measures which the government has already taken and will be taking, and considerable conservation measures on the part of the provinces. Some provinces think energy conservation is purely a provincial responsibility. It will require a much greater degree of urgency on the part of the government of Alberta with respect to the development of the tar sands.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY INTO BREAK-INS AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE AND PRAXIS CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I moved earlier, seconded by another member of the House, that there be a judicial inquiry with respect to this matter. I moved it in good faith because I believe it is extremely important, not only from the point of view of the government, but certainly from the point of view of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Is it the intention of the government to have a ministerial statement in this House which will take the place of a judicial inquiry? Is this announcement this morning by the Prime Minister an indication the Prime Minister has decided today that there is no possibility and no need for a judicial inquiry with respect to this matter, and only a statement would suffice?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY INTO BREAK-INS AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE AND PRAXIS CORPORATION
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that. It may be entirely possible or desirable that a judicial inquiry follow. To be perfectly candid, I discussed this very matter with the Commissioner of the RCMP when the facts first came to my attention about the laying of charges against one of their former officers for illegal break-in and entry. I came to the conclusion then, and I have stated it to the House on many occasions, that I prefer, through due process, a judicial procedure to follow its course. If the opposition can, with absolute justification, claim all the facts are not known, then I will certainly consider setting up a federal inquiry.
My position in this House has always been that we do not set up inquiries if due process can bring the facts and the guilty persons to light. I do not see any reason for making an exception for the RCMP and to start an inquiry on them if the judicial process, which is operating in Montreal and in Toronto on the two cases in question, is going to bring the facts to light.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Does the Prime Minister have that in mind, and will he bear those limitations in mind, in terms of the judicial process, when he is considering the question of a judicial inquiry which has a much broader scope?

If the people accused then plead guilty, it seems to demonstrate the police have done their work effectively and have traced the accusations to the proper people.

Someone just said that the questions of the new Minister without Portfolio go back to November. I should like to see some answers to his questions. I suggest the government has been negligent. We are entitled to know why the parliamentary secretary has asked that these questions be allowed to stand. Are the questions too complicated to answer? Is that why some were not answered yesterday, the day before, and today? We are entitled to know. I can understand this happening once, but when it happens three days in a row we are entitled to an explanation. Many of the questions are neither long nor complicated. As I have said,
Order Paper Questions

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order and support wholeheartedly what both my colleagues have said. May I suggest something constructive? If the government fails to answer a question within a specific time, say within two weeks or a month of its being set down, the parliamentary secretary should explain the reason for the delay. I say this for a particular reason. Constituents often ask members of parliament to raise such questions because information furnished in the answers influences business decisions. I have had experience of this.
If the government does not release the information or is tardy in answering questions, the end result may be that business opportunities are lost. If the parliamentary secretary, after two weeks or one month, could explain why the question has not been answered, the member or his constituent could seek other channels of information. If the government cannot answer an order paper question within a couple of weeks, say, I suggest someone in authority should immediately communicate with the member of parliament asking the question and say why the question cannot be answered within a reasonable period.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-17, respecting the reorganization of Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last we discussed two bills to do with air transport, the aeronautics bill, which we passed, and Bill C-17 dealing with the reorganization of Air Canada. As I said on Wednesday, this government's approach to transportation policy is fundamentally wrong. One week we discuss freight rates, another week a bill on railways, and another week a bill on airlines. Clearly, this country needs a comprehensive transportation policy which will promote the most efficient way of moving people and goods, encourage the conservation of energy, reduce pollution and make the most efficient use of manpower. We must use our airlines, railways, trucks, buses and private cars in the most efficient manner. This we have not done. By introducing bills of this sort the government is putting off, perhaps for years, the time when we can draw up the necessary and comprehensive plans which will enable us to use most efficiently all modes of transportation.
As I said on Wednesday, this simple bill will change the structure of Air Canada. On Wednesday we gave second reading to Bill C-46 to amend the Aeronautics Act. I suppose we shall today give Bill C-17 second reading. This bill merely changes the organization of Air Canada. Mr. Speaker, we are considering this legislation in isolation, as it were, ignoring the tremendous changes taking place, particularly in the field of air transport. Those changes have taken place without sparking any discussion in parliament. So far as I know, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has not made a single public statement on what is happening or what is the government's position. Obviously, some changes could not take place if the government did not approve. We do not know the basis for some changes or what their effect will be.
In this regard I direct the attention of hon. members to an important change taking place in the field of air transportation. Hon. members who read today's edition of the Montreal Gazette no doubt will have noted that Pacific Western Airlines has completed a deal to purchase Transair. I mentioned on Wednesday that had the minister possessed the authority which he will possess when the aeronautics bill is passed, he would have prevented the government of Alberta from pur-

chasing Pacific Western Airlines. That is a power he will have when we complete the passage of the aeronautics bill to which we gave second reading on Wednesday.
I am not opposed, as the minister for some considerable time said he was, to the idea of a provincial government getting into the air transportation business. I find it interesting that the minister should now have agreed to the expansion of Pacific Western Airlines, although it is owned by a provincial government, and I wonder what his response would have been and what the response of members of the official opposition would have been had it been the NDP government of British Columbia which had purchased PWA instead of the Conservative government of Alberta. However, that purchase has been made and, as I say, we are not opposed to provincial governments being in the air transportation business. But now Pacific Western Airlines, owned by the Alberta government, is proceeding to complete a deal through which it will purchase Transair. Transair is a company based in Winnipeg. It has a route into northern Ontario, a route between Winnipeg and Toronto, a route into the Northwest Territories. Suddenly we find that the Minister of Transport, who was long opposed to the government of Alberta purchasing PWA, approves and encourages the deal. Apparently he has given some commitment, verbal at least, that there would be sweeteners to Pacific Western Airlines if it put this deal through. One newspaper story said that PWA was purchasing Transair for less than it would cost the company to purchase one new DC-10.
It is interesting they should be able to do this and that they should be doing it with the approval of the Minister of Transport. According to the Winnipeg Free Press of May 10, the Premier of Manitoba, in which province the airline has its business office and overhaul facilities, was not shown the courtesy of being informed by the Minister of Transport of what was taking place or what had been agreed to. The Winnipeg Free Press reports that at the sitting of the legislature, when the news had become public, Premier Schreyer said he would raise with the federal minister some disturbing questions about the merger. The news story goes on to say:
He told the legislature he had tried in vain to reach Lang Monday because he intended to speak to him that day.

probably flying around.

Schreyer said he was told by federal officials that the merger hung on whether Transair would give up its Toronto-Winnipeg run in return for some of Air Canada's viable western routes. He told the legislature this raised some disturbing questions about why such routes were not offered to Transair previously.
Mr. Speaker, surely when we are discussing a bill about Air Canada, the Minister of Transport could have used his time while introducing the measure to tell us which western routes Air Canada would be turning over to Pacific Western Airlines. Surely the minister could have given some information to the Premier of Manitoba who, according to the Prime Minister
May 27, 1977

(Mr. Trudeau), has been more willing to think as a Canadian rather than as premier of one province than any other premier in this country. Yet he did not even show him the courtesy of telling him what kind of deal he was making behind his back. This is a deal which is just completed, and it is one about which we ought to be given a good deal of information.
Today's Montreal Gazette carries a story on the front page of its business section, the headline of which reads: "Sale of CP Air to Pacific Western under discussion: federal official". Let me quote a couple of paragraphs from the story by Nicholas Hills.
Pacific Western, the Alberta government-owned airline will next take control of CP Air, the money-losing subsidiary of Canadian Pacific Limited, industry sources say.
The story goes on:
Rumour or not, good airline or not, there is one inescapable fact: Canadian Pacific is fed up with its airline losing money. The losses of $9.8 million in 1975-76 and $6.4 million in 1974-75 are a drag on the giant's corporate image, let alone its books.
With its recent acquisition of Transair Limited of Winnipeg, PWA is now the second airline in the country. It basically controls regional air travel in the west and runs head-to-head against CP Air on many DC routes including those into Prince George, Terrace and Prince Rupert.
It may make some sense to have competition on those routes, but if PWA purchases CP Air it will be in direct competition on the transcontinental route with Air Canada. So you will have the strange position of one airline owned by the federal government which carries passengers from Victoria to St. John's and another airline, PWA, owned by the Alberta government which will be moving passengers from Victoria to Montreal, both of which, in the last couple of years, have been losing money.
Hon. members to my right cannot say everybody knows that a government-owned operation cannot be run efficiently so we should not be surprised it is losing money. Here we have a privately-owned airline which has lost money in the last two years. There are several reasons for this. First, there is the tremendous increase in the cost of fuel, an increase in the neighbourhood of 300 per cent. Every airline in the world is in trouble, and virtually every airline, whether owned by its government or privately, is now being subsidized. That is part of the reason. The other part of the reason is the cost of air travel. Most planes flying in Canada and in other countries have substantial excess capacity, to the extent of having 30, 40 or even 50 per cent of their seats unfilled. This raises another question which we should examine.
The original decision of the Conservative government, which was expanded by the Liberal government, was to have competition, to have two airlines operating on transcontinental routes across Canada. We wonder whether this was a wise policy or whether we would not have been better off to follow the policy elaborated under a Liberal government by that great businessman and free enterpriser, C. D. Howe, where one transcontinental airline owned and operated by the people of Canada would operate in Canada for service and not for profit.
Air Canada
The acquisition of Transair by PWA will have vital consequences for the people of western Canada, regardless whether PWA is privately owned, as it was until a few years ago, or publicly owned, as it is now by the government of Alberta. The possible acquisition by PWA of CP Air will also have tremendous consequences for the people of Canada. I suggest that the least the people of Canada have the right to expect from the Minister of Transport is that he should tell them what is happening and explain the decisions that have been reached. If consideration has been given by CP Air to sell the company to Pacific Western Airlines, then what is the position of the government of Canada, and what are the reasons for the sale?
We have had not a word from the minister in this regard. He does not want discussion of public issues. He wants to make decisions in consultation with a few senior bureaucrats in his department, who have been consistently wrong on many of the most important decisions which have been made, as well, 1 suppose, as in consultation with some of the big business executives with whom the minister is obviously much more comfortable than he is with members of parliament or members of the public.
These are matters which need to be discussed now but which should have been discussed long before. This minister should have given us an explanation when he introduced the bill on Wednesday, rather than non-committal chatting concerning a few details. Until we have this kind of discussion of transportation and air policy, the members of this party will oppose this bill and any others which the minister brings forth.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate on Bill C-17 I am rather compelled to repeat what I said in the House during debate on Bill C-54, the excise tax bill which we discussed last week. At that time I said that this government has shown a remarkable knack for bringing legislation before the House the provisions of which, for reasons known only to the government, end up 180 degrees off course.
The bill before the House today says, in effect, that Air Canada has what Air Canada's management feels is an uncomfortable weight of debt and somehow Air Canada should be restructured so as to relieve the corporation of the carrying charges of that debt. That is a nice way to express it. As we know, Air Canada officials have often come forward in committee and said they feel that if they were freed from the debt load they would be able to show relatively better earnings.
Having made that point, it is interesting how those who believe in state-run enterprises like Air Canada and love to posture this type of activity also love to cloud the issue and to disguise the mismanagement which is usually found in most state-run operations. The hard fact is that the reason Air Canada has such a heavy debt, which is owing to the government of Canada through the CNR, is that they have been running substantial losses. They are now comparing their operation with comparable airlines in the United States, and they say that the capital ratios in the United States so far as debt is concerned are higher than their ratio; that somehow

May 27, 1977
Air Canada
this should be adjusted almost magically by the government's accepting the capitalization of the debt owing to them.
The point the minister does not make clear, and the point the officials of Air Canada do not make clear either, is that the capital ratio they refer to in respect of private carriers in the United States was not something given to those concerns by a government. It was not something that was even paid in in the main by the shareholders of those concerns. It was the accumulated earnings which those airlines were able to build up over the years which gave them the wherewithal to be effective, viable entities in sharp contrast to Air Canada.
Later in my remarks I want to draw a contrast, for example, between Air Canada and Northwest Airlines, which is a very similar operation run, of course, as a private concern in the United States. In these two cases roughly the same revenue pours into the companies, roughly the same number of air miles are flown, and roughly the same number of aeroplanes are owned by the two companies. But Northwest Airlines made, in the period to which I shall be referring later, a profit of about $100 million, whereas Air Canada lost $20 million.
The number one point which stands out in contrast when you compare those two companies is the number of staff of the two airlines. Air Canada, with an approximate revenue equal to that of Northwest Airlines, has almost double the number of employees Northwest Airlines has. To me, that, in a nutshell, is the problem with state-run enterprises. Profit is not a motive. They realize they have government coffers to fall back on, so if it is a question of hiring a few more people, why not? The fact is that when a bureaucrat sees evidence of profit in a Crown corporation, he almost gets into a state of hysteria in making sure expenses increase fast enough so that the profit will not continue.
One of the things I am concerned about in the bill before us is that if we capitalize this debt, which is really notional, there will not even be notional charging of interest by the government to Air Canada from now on. In short, if this notional debt of Air Canada stands at, say, $70 million, just think what a boon it will be to Air Canada. If that is capitalized, they will no longer have to reflect that interest cost and, in short, they will be given a $60 million to $70 million subsidization by the government of Canada. Mark my words, if Air Canada is allowed to continue with no further restriction and no attempt to privatize it or somehow make it more conscious of the need to earn a profit, that subsidization will be used up in a matter of years and they will be back into a deficit position with some new rationalization as to why they are not viable.
Having made those few preliminary remarks, I would like to state that in the excise bill I have referred to we saw where the government somehow managed to devise a tax on tourism. I am referring to the air transportation tax. They devised that tax at a time when our travel accounts are in critical deficit. I am pleased the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is in the House. I notice he is reading his green paper-I hope not for

the first time-on the decontrol mechanism which he is intending to explain at a press conference later this afternoon.
Is it not odd, when we have run up a $1.2 billion tourist deficit in this country and when the Financial Post estimates if the trend continues it could be a $10 billion deficit some time in the 1980s, that the government chooses this time to bring in a foreign air transportation tax to cover what they say are the user costs of the airport facilities? As was raised at the time the excise bill was before us, the fact is that the costs they refer to are in many ways costs we do not have to incur in this country. Airports could run on a profitable basis if there were better direction at the Ottawa level.
As far as the government's actions are concerned, we saw their refusal to abolish or decrease the sales tax on smaller, more energy-efficient cars. That was a measure which we felt would spur the economy and provide a direct and positive incentive to energy conservation. We saw this 180-degree turnaround as far as the government is concerned in this bill which is now up for debate at second reading. This is a bill which is supposedly designed to put Air Canada on a viable commercial and financial basis competitive with privately-run airlines. In essence, it would bring Air Canada under increasingly direct government control. It is an anomaly, I would suggest, of this administration which can be so successful at drafting legislation totally and completely opposed to the very spirit and aims which produced the legislation in the first place.
Few, if any, in this House wish to see Air Canada limping along with its wings clipped back by continuing losses. They have even given up their peanuts on certain of the flights which I have been on. I do not know whether it was because they were being called internationally the "peanut airline" or whether this is another measure of restraint on their part.

My colleague from the other party says they are mad at Jimmy Carter. That may be so, but I am not sure. Be that as it may, I do not think anyone wants to see a state-run operation such as Air Canada in a loss position. That is not a good advertisement for the nation. The losses Air Canada is referring to have grown in the past three years from $9.2 million in 1974 to $13 million in 1975, and last year the loss was down a bit, to $10.4 million. All of us, with the possible exception of the socialists to my left, want to see Air Canada operate on a sound, efficient and profitable footing. In this connection, at least, we support those provisions which would reduce Air Canada's staggering debt equity ratio and reduce its cost of financing.
Having said that, I would emphasize that hon. members should take a good, solid look at why that debt structure has been allowed to arise in Air Canada and should not assume it was something which could not have been avoided. What is astounding is that the government would pursue these laudable

goals in the framework of the legislation before us today, that is, the framework of Bill C-17 which has the laudable goal of trying to put Air Canada on a more viable basis. I would say the framework is not suitable for what the government claims they are attempting to do.
At present we have in this country an estimated 1,200 state-owned and operated concerns. Few, if any, of these are models of efficiency or sound financial management. One need only read the Auditor General's report to confirm what I am saying. Yet the government is proposing today that we get Air Canada to straighten up and fly right by removing it from the control of the Canadian National Railways and placing it firmly under the control of the Minister of Transport. In our minds, this is taking our national airline from the frying pan and pitching it squarely into the fire. Hon. members must remember who it is that is proposing to run Air Canada.

Hon. members will recall that the government, in the Speech from the Throne and again in the white paper entitled "The Way Ahead", promised increased reliance on the private sector. It was stated in the throne speech:
In a further effort to reduce the size of government as well as expand the range of opportunities for private enterprise, all federal programs will be reviewed to identify those government activities which could be transferred to the private sector without reducing the quality of service to the public.
Later in the speech the government again promised to "promote greater freedom and efficiency in the marketplace." Still later, in defence of its so called "middle road" between complete reliance on the free market and socialist intervention in the system, the government stated:
-that choice also implies that the working of the market must be improved and that less costly, less interventionist ways must be found to pursue social goals.
We welcomed these words, hoping they signalled a return to sanity, a recognition that the economy could sustain no more excessive government flab and grab. Subsequently, when successive news reports indicated the minister was investigating means of turning over Air Canada to private hands, we thought this would be the logical place to begin a constructive diminution of government control. Frankly, we were interested to see what would be the government's suggested method of making Air Canada a private enterprise. After all, the minister himself stated in his opening remarks to this bill: "Air Canada is no longer a fledging airline and no longer needs special protective measures". We had hoped that by preparing Air Canada-now 40 years old-to fly on its own, the government was setting the pace for other divestment of unnecessary state ownership. But we were wrong, for when we examine this bill we find that Air Canada has been merely shifted to ministerial management. We have only the minister's word that such direct government management will result in sound commercial and financial viability. As I said, given the track record of this minister and his government, that word is not enough.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was stating that I felt in some ways members must be quite sharp in their observations concerning the bill before us, in that I think it is once again the type of rationalization that the government likes to go through to cover mistakes in the operations of one of the Crown corporations, in this case Air Canada.
I should like to state, also, that I believe the provisions of Bill C-17 are so wide and encompassing that the cabinet will have virtually complete control over the board of directors of Air Canada if the legislation goes through in the form in which it is now before us. Cloaked in language that purports a new era of Air Canada competition with private airlines, the bill, in its very broadness, merely points the way to massive interventions in the operation of Air Canada. In the minister's own words, the bill "provides for direct government ownership"; and, again, "Air Canada would be required to comply with direction from the governor in council." This direct ministerial control over Air Canada is unfortunate. It is businessmen, not bureaucrats, who know how to run a commercially successful enterprise.
The specifics of this new arrangement as far as the bill and the minister's speech are concerned are to come at a later date. But given the fact that the government has failed to bring the annual report of Air Canada for each of the three previous years before committee, we can only surmise that it will be even harder to scrutinize the airline's operations under the cloak of ministerial privilege. Clearly, the government is playing a game of monopoly again and, as usual, it spells out the rules only as it suits them and only when it suits their timing. It is playing monopoly with billions of taxpayers' dollars, secure in the knowledge that a multimillion blunder here or there will not break them as it would private industry. Being government, it can simply send taxpayers digging deeper into their pockets to cover government mistakes.
The government is playing big business with all the assets of what will surely be one of the world's most lavishly capitalized airlines-and I emphasize this. It will not have the risk, as far as operation is concerned, that most of the world's airlines have to accept as privately-run companies. It will be one of the world's most lavishly capitalized airlines, as I have stated, if this bill goes through. Frankly, we cannot find another airline that will have such naked capital to work with as Air Canada will if the amendment proposed by the minister sees the light of day.
May 27, 1977

It is an approach we have seen all too often in this House. The government, with their fondness for Crown corporations- as we know, they are planning two more in VIA rail and marine transport-are acting as would-be "captains of industry" with someone else's money. Too often these experiments go sour and prove to be wasteful and expensive exercises in bureaucratic bungling. Frequently, they are counterproductive and even hurt the industries they are supposed to be helping and, in some cases, spearheading development-PetroCan, for example. Sometimes they are even swollen and flabby retreats for party faithful: an incorporated pork-barrel of incompetence and privilege. Our experience with these state-run companies in the past clearly shows that what is needed for Air Canada is not another Crown corporation but systematic and phased conversion into a private concern. Free market competition and management by those who have a personal stake in the enterprise would get our national airline off the ground again and back into the profit column.
I referred earlier to the comparisons that can be made between the operational losses of Air Canada and the profits being made by private carriers in North America. Some time ago I saw a report that Northwest Airlines had a net profit of some $60 million in 1974. What struck me was not that Northwest had made a profit-that is fairly common among the privately-run American airlines-but, rather, that on closer examination we see that Northwest is similar in size and operation to Air Canada. Both operated in 1975 with revenues of under $1 billion. In Air Canada's case it was $957 million, and in Northwest's case it was slightly more than $800 million. Both operate the same size fleet, covering similar route distances. Air Canada ran 120 aircraft in 1975, while Northwest ran 113. Both pay, with two major exceptions, similar operational expenditures, including rental expenses which in 1975 were $10.4 million for Air Canada and $10.6 million for Northwest Airlines. Where they differ, however, is in profit- and they differ there in a shocking way. Northwest made more than $100 million in two years, while Air Canada incurred net losses of $22 million in the same two years.
Why is that, Mr. Speaker? Surely, when considering Bill C-17-which in a sense is a cover-up of the previous loss Air Canada has been incurring-we must ask ourselves why this airline has so consistently been in a loss position. No doubt there are several reasons, but chief among them is the fact that Northwest Airlines operated with a staff of slightly more than one-half that of Air Canada-11,268, compared to Air Canada's 21,293. Second, Northwest was faced with long-term debt financing amounting to $271.9 million in 1975, while Air Canada was saddled with more than $1 billion.
The 1975 Air Canada annual report drives home the importance of these two operating expenses. On page 3 we find that "wages and benefits rose by $45 million that year or 13 per cent and accounted for 45 per cent of the increase in operating expenses in 1975." On page 4 we find that "long-term debt increase rose by more than $8 million or 11 per cent". Page 5 of the report says that "if Air Canada had a more conventional
Air Canada
debt-equity ratio the company would have reduced expenses by more than $30 million and would have shown a net profit of about $2.9 million." Mr. Speaker, these two excessive expenditures, bloated payrolls and astronomical debt, are commonplace among Crown corporations and this, I believe, is the real story behind Air Canada's plight.
I referred to Northwest Airlines, and some may think I singled out a certain airline in the United States for unfair comparison. But I could refer equally well to other American air carriers, either bigger or smaller than Air Canada. In Moody's reports I cannot find a scheduled airline in the United States operating at a loss.

speechtext:
Yet here Air Canada is telling us that it needs to convert its debt in order to make a profit. Consider the position of American Airlines Incorporated. It made a net profit of $56 million on total revenues of approximately $2 billion. Interestingly enough, American Airlines have retained earnings of $263 million. Their capital, incidentally, is $28 million and they have a paid-in surplus in addition. American Airlines in past years earned enough to pay taxes, pay dividends and retain earnings. Its retained earnings position at the end of last year was $263 million. Consider Air Canada's balance sheet. As of December 31 last year, Air Canada had retained earnings of $18 million. Contrast those retained earnings with the $263 million in retained earnings of American Airlines. In addition, Air Canada borrowed extensively from the government of Canada. It needed to borrow money, not having accumulated retained earnings.
Now it says to the government, "Do not ask us to pay interest any longer on the debt. We will be better off if you increase our capitalization and do not ask us to pay interest." There is an important contrast in all this. American Airlines has been able to accumulate capital, whereas Air Canada has not. American Airlines has followed the free enterprise approach, not the socialist or bureaucratic approach. Operating under principles of private enterprise, the airline competed, earned money and accumulated capital, which in turn will permit it to be more profitable in future. We can do the same. More profits will mean more jobs for Canadians. Unfortunately, few state-run operations have the incentive to drive for profits and earnings.
Let me mention other airlines. Eastern Airlines, in the year ended last December, made a net profit of $46 million on total operating revenues of $1.8 billion. Let there be no doubt: the company must pay interest on its debt; it borrowed from the general public, not from Washington. It went for its funds to the open market. I touch on this point to emphasize that the loss figures of Air Canada show only part of the story.
Air Canada, the largest air carrier in the country, is the biggest user of our airports. Our airports are subsidized and to that extent the airport subsidy is a subsidy for Air Canada. Air Canada benefits from the subsidy to the extent it uses subsidized airports. I suggest, in this regard, the government hides

May 27, 1977
Air Canada
from Canadians the true cost of Air Canada operations and the misoperation of our airports.
I said earlier that the Post Office was marginally profitable in 1970. Apparently it is running a deficit of about $700 million. The same is true of our airports. Our airports were run profitably in 1970, but they are currently being run about $100 million in the red if you include the Mirabel loss of $56 million a year. This must stop. We, as members of parliament, must press the government to be more prudent with Canadian taxpayers' money. I say this because when the government gets into difficulty, it tends to favour its Crown corporations, or it requires Crown corporations to bail it out, so to speak. Let me give some examples. Not long ago, for reasons still not clear, the Department of Transport built terminal 2 in Toronto. Please remember that Air Canada and other carriers had used terminal 1. The department built terminal 2, expecting international carriers to use it. When the terminal was completed and the international carriers learned how expensive it would be to use terminal 2, they told the government they would not use it. There was no way American Airlines, KLM, Lufthansa and other international carriers were going to use terminal 2, because it was exorbitantly expensive.
What happened? The government turned to Air Canada, a Crown corporation, and told it to use terminal 2. That terminal is probably the most unsatisfactory terminal of its kind in North America, and Air Canada is forced to use it because it is a Crown corporation. Therefore, because the other carriers refused to use terminal 2, Air Canada was forced to use that white elephant. 1 could give many examples to show the unfortunate relationship between government and Crown corporations. Let me give a second example to show how effectively and efficiently airports are used in the United States. In that country all airports come under the jurisdiction of local authorities. For example, the New York airport authority has jurisdiction over Kennedy international airport, LaGuardia and Newark. Those airports all make money, and the reason is simple. Before an airport is extended or a new airport built, the local authority seeks the assurance of carriers who will use the airports that the airport will generate sufficient revenues to retire the debt to be incurred for carrying out the improvements or extensions.
We do not do this in Canada. The government of Canada, operating in a centralized way, hands down a decision from Ottawa to Montreal, Vancouver, Toronto, Calgary, Edmonton, and so on. The government makes up its mind as to what facility should be built, finances the building of the facility and is surprised when carriers say, "We cannot make a profit from the new facility" and refuse to use it. The next step is to turn to the Canadian public and say, "Now you must pay user tax to make up for our mistakes". Why should we be ending up with the largest airports in North America being financed at the cost of the taxpayers or of those using the airports? The Chicago airport authority told me, for example, that they do not intend to build additional facilities in Chicago, as far as they can see, until 1990 or 2000 because they do not think they will need them. Here we are speaking of O'Hare airport in

Chicago which is handling seven times the number of passengers that are using Malton. But the Department of Transport is saying a new airport is needed in Toronto, notwithstanding the fact there is only one-seventh of the activity there is in Chicago, where they say frankly that they cannot afford a new airport.

I thank hon. members for their courtesy. I shall be brief. It is a common trend, I would suggest, for companies such as I have been referring to-Air Canada, for example-to run up huge expenses. They go heavily into debt and eventually they come to us saying, "Let us off the hook". One need only compare the poor performance of Air Canada with that of Northwest Airlines or, for that matter, any other U.S. or privately-run airline such as North Central, Braniff, Southern Airways or Eastern Airlines, to see the difference which private control makes.
Leaner operations, smaller staffs, more efficient management-these are the trademarks of private enterprise, as opposed to enterprises run by public agencies commonly known as Crown corporations. I stated earlier there are now more than 1,200 federally-owned concerns in Canada, and we are still counting. To date we have poured more than $21 million into these enterprises, including hundreds of millions of dollars sunk into Air Canada. I suggest it is time to stop counting and to start subtracting. It is time to begin divesting ourselves of some of these Crown corporations, rather than creating new ones.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last statement made by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) is a significant one not only in terms of the present number of Crown agencies and corporations but in terms of suggested approach to national problems. If you look at developments in the last few years, Mr. Speaker, I believe you will agree with me that whenever there is a problem, whether it involves a certain field of business, transportation or whatever, governments everywhere, and this government in particular, appear to have decided that the only answer is an approach by way of a different from of the public service, namely, the Crown corporation.
I am not arguing that there is no place within the structure of a nation for government agencies, but there has been a growing temptation to look toward the public sector as an easy way out. I cannot believe that a country as vibrant as ours is supposed to be, or could be, a country as rich in human and material resources as ours, must go back to what I call a bottom line position, one which suggests that business does not have the initiative or the spark or the trustworthiness to secure the desired objectives. Unfortunately, this is an attitude which is easy to promote.
May 27, 1977

This morning we heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) trying to justify the operations of a Crown agency by saying that even airlines in the private sector are finding themselves in difficulty today.

speechtext:
This afternoon he had the
opportunity to hear a speech by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe who clearly showed that generalization to be untrue. Now that the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) has decided to interject by mentioning Canadian Pacific, I would remind him that the article to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North referred contained an interesting passage. Talking about the position of CP Air, that article had something to say which is of particular relevance to this argument. Perhaps the position of a private airline trying to compete against an airline whose operation is controlled by the government is an unique one. I quote from the article:
Apart from the fact that it is only allowed a quarter of the domestic market, CP Air finds itself on the outside looking in on many fat international routes. And even after it has won a lucrative service, Ottawa often dilutes the economic effect.
The Vancouver-based airline's service into the San Francisco, Los Angeles area is a case in point. This was a good money-maker for CP Air until the Liberal government allowed Air Canada to fly into the same region from Alberta thus syphoning off all those passengers who used to fly from Edmonton and Calgary to Vancouver and then take CP Air into California.
I am not standing here as an advocate of CP Air. They can be the advocates of their own cause. What I am saying is that the hon. member's remarks ought not to mislead us because, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe mentioned, many of these privately-owned airlines, enterprises which do not have unlimited funds upon which to draw, which have payrolls to meet and which pay taxes, federal, state and municipal, are making a profit. It is folly to say it cannot be done. It may be the case that CP Air finds itself in a little difficult position when it must compete, even on the level I have mentioned, with an airline operated by a government which has an all-pervading authority in regard to where that carrier may operate.
I started by saying that I had listened very carefully to the speech of my colleague, who I think has put his finger on one of the problems, namely, the belief there is in this country that only the government can carry out operations efficiently. The bill under consideration separates Air Canada from the Canadian National Railways, something for which the Progressive Conservative party has asked for over a period of many years. There is nothing at all wrong with the attempt being made to diversify the operations of Air Canada so it can pursue related areas of endeavour. But what concerns me is the demonstrated inefficiency of this government to manage its business enterprises, on the one hand, and, as the Auditor General has pointed out, the inability of this government to operate in an efficient accounting way.
This proposed diversification will be carried out under the aegis of a board of directors which will be appointed by, and subject to the direction of, the very group of men and women
Air Canada
in this country who have been castigated by the Auditor General as among the most inefficient administrators in the history of this country. That is the tragedy of this piece of legislation. I look upon it as something we will have to watch. We will have to see that this board of directors does not become merely a convenient burial ground for the party faithful.
The Minister of Transport has said that diversification is a good thing, and I happen to agree. But if Air Canada is going to diversify, if it is going to change its share structure so it can compete equally in a financial way with other corporations, if it is to be subject to the same licensing provisions and its objects are to be broadened, and if, as someone said earlier in this debate, it is going to get off its knees and start to run instead of walk, and perhaps to fly, then I do not think the public of this country are going to stand by and watch the same failure of management which has befallen other Crown corporations and government operations.
Is there anything in the proposals in this bill which indicates that all of a sudden, because of a restructuring of Air Canada and its objects, there is going to be a different check made of its operations on behalf of the people of Canada, who will have to carry the freight for the present deficit, or for deficits which are to come-because there is no indication that the government is going to change its operation, except on paper?
Is there any indication that this parliament is going to be treated in any different way in terms of its being able to call upon this Crown corporation, to a large extent operated by public funds, to account? Can we be assured by this bill that it will become the rule of both law and tradition that this Crown corporation will automatically have its annual reports and financial statements sent to a committee of this House to be questioned, persued and examined? Is there any provision in this bill providing that Air Canada officials will be any more subject to scrutiny under the rules of this House than they are today? Not one word, not one whit, Mr. Speaker.
There is nothing in this piece of legislation which in any way gets at the heart of the operations of this Crown corporation and others. So do not let anyone think that this bill is the last word. It is far from that. There is some question that it is even the first word regarding what has to be done about the operations of this government in a field which is successfully occupied in North America by the private sector. Let not one member sit back and think that things are going to be any different.
What else does the bill provide? Is there to be an independent board of directors? No, Mr. Speaker. The board of directors will be the creature of the government. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) will be able to stand up, like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and other ministers, and say, "I have nothing to say about this; it is in the hands of the board of directors of Air Canada". Therefore, he will be able to slough-off ministerial responsibility for the corporation, as is the case with a whole host of other corporations. All of us have had questions answered in this way in the House.

May 27, 1977
Air Canada
In terms of the auditing provisions of the bill, when the minister made his speech in the House on May 25 he said, as reported at page 5945 of Hansard:
Associated with this change, the present arrangement whereby the auditors of CN are by legislation also the auditors for Air Canada should be discontinued. Therefore the bill provides for the appointment of Air Canada's auditors by the governor in council-
What assurance to the House is that in terms of financial accounting? Auditors for other organizations have been appointed by the governor in council, but no annual reports from some of those organizations have been before the committee. In spite of this kind of appointment, what did the Auditor General say about it? He said that the financial accounting of this government and the use of public funds- these are almost his words-has amounted to a breach of public trust. What assurance does this bill give that there will be any change? None whatsoever.
Those are some of the questions which will have to be examined in a much broader way when this bill goes to committee. I do not believe the people of Canada any longer believe that with respect to management of business affairs which could be just as well left to the private sector the government has done as well, or that any government could do as well, as properly motivated people in the private sector.
As a result of the movement of governments at all levels toward becoming involved in what was normally the preserve, reasonably regulated of course, but nevertheless the preserve, of the private sector, legitimate profit has become a dirty word. Reasonable profit has become a dirty phrase. It is now improper for a businessman to say that it is reasonable for him to make a profit. The party to my left are always attacking the large multinational corporations and seem to forget that the business people of this country, in terms of employment and generation of jobs, are not the large multinational corporations but men and women who are prepared to put their life savings, what they can borrow, their hopes and reputations behind an enterprise. That kind of philosophy ought to be fostered in this country, not subjected to pressure. It is important that we put out of our minds the concept that the truth is that government by itself has all the answers to all the problems and challenges facing this country.
We consider it is the job of government to create the atmosphere where men and women who so desire can run risks, make reasonable returns and from time to time losses, in order to realize their capabilities. It is this kind of philosophy which seems to be overtaking governments-the easy way out, the unlimited treasury and the unlimited deficits, which have sickened this country and weakened it. There is a whole host of problems, not just the ones which afflict us in the private sector.
This bill is going to be examined very carefully in committee. It is a reflection of a continuing sickness in terms of the attitude of governments generally. This government has been in power for a long time. During that time Crown corporations have not gone down in number but have increased, and Crown

agencies have not diminished but have increased. Why? It is because this government has decided that is the direction in which it will go. It will intervene, instead of asking the question: Is there some other way the job can be done just as well, and not place the burden upon the taxpayers of this country? This House and this country should examine that attitude and not just this bill.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this bill entitled An Act respecting the reorganization of Air Canada. The main purpose of this bill is to select means of transport properly. We have already done it by selecting Via Rail, an independent body for freight transportation, which is a great improvement within the CNR system. Today the government introduces a bill providing that Air Canada becomes a Crown corporation separate from the CNR. I think that after 40 years, Mr. Speaker, it is time for Air Canada to become an adult company that will manage its own affairs.
The first few years will not be easy as it is already burdened with over a billion-and then some hundred million-dollar deficit; fortunately, Air Canada will be able to get, in addition to the $25 million in share capital and the $750 million in authorized capital provided for under the current legislation, a direct loan of $750 million guaranteed by the state. Finally, if necessary it will be allowed under the new legislation to borrow on its own credit. Air Canada will enter areas of operation which are related to air transport, like tourism. We shall remain the true owners of Air Canada, with everything this entails, and I refer immediately to the expected deficit. We have learned through experience that Crown corporations are very difficult to administer. They are more expensive to operate than private corporations, but our system is made up of public and private firms and we are faced now with the need to re-organize transports, something which I feel is most necessary in Canada today. Still I am very glad we had to deal with this bill today.
Besides, we all would be happy if Air Canada were for once to belie the saying that private companies are always more profitable than state-owned ones. The corporation will be under the management of a board of directors comprised of a chairman appointed pursuant to subclause 5 and at least thirteen other directors to be appointed for a term not exceeding three years.
We are anxious, Mr. Speaker, to know the successful candidates to find out whether the minister will abide by his government's bilingualism policy. I happened to check the bill to see which qualifications the directors and board members should have. Here is what it says about those qualifications:
(2) No person is eligible to be appointed or to continue as a member of the Board ...
That is the first qualification: to continue as a member.
Here is the second:
.. . who
May 27, 1977

(a)	is not a Canadian citizen ordinarily resident in Canada; or
(b)	has attained the age of seventy years.
I thought it was sixty-five, but we read "the age of seventy years".
I remain somewhat puzzled because nowhere is there any reference to language requirements in the choice of those people, and yet that would be very important considering the bilingualism policy advocated by the government. There should at least be a short clause requiring the majority of directors to be bilingual. That is my criticism. I say that to the minister so that the question might be raised and discussed in committee because when the matter of bilingualism is not included in a legislation, we are likely to face many difficulties. Everyone is aware of the difficulties we had about the application of bilingualism and the use of French in this Crown corporation over which the government seems to have lost control. All members surely recall the notorious case of the Gens de fair, CATCA and CALPA, which is not yet solved, as we are still waiting for the decision of the various courts because the government cannot apparently decide anything by itself; they have to have this decision made by a court.
Today we see that there is still much room for improvement as far as bilingualism in Air Canada workshops is concerned, both among air traffic controllers and aircraft servicing personnel. Air Canada has certainly not shown much enthusiasm to try at least to submit to the will of the government. 1 see that the government is willing to force Air Canada to act but I think they do not take the means to do so. Again, I hope that the committee will discuss the possibility of including this matter of bilingualism in the bill once for all. We have been talking about bilingualism for years. I think this matter will remain a dead letter, as long as we talk about it, as long as it will not be included in a piece of legislation requiring that this or that group is bilingual or unilingual, or that it should at least try to learn the other language.
I think we have had enough problems, and the air pilots issue has still not been settled. We have had all the trouble in the world to solve that bilingualism problem, and all we got was the threat by the pilots' union to prevent French Canadians in Quebec from using their language in the air. Everybody said it was a scandal, and they were right. I think we have a good opportunity to discuss it here, while we are dealing with this bill to transform Air Canada into a Crown corporation independent from the Canadian National. If we miss this opportunity to insert in the law what the present government advocates throughout Canada, we will again postpone the settlement of the bilingualism issue and permit certain associations to quarrel between themselves and make the Canadian people suffer because they are too stubborn. I therefore hope to see this obligation included in the bill, because if it were the other way around, if English were at stake, if the survival of the English language were threatened, I am sure the problem would have been solved a long time ago.
In the meantime, we are told that both languages are recognized in Canada, and the government has launched its bilingualism campaign. I do not see why this would not be
Air Canada
included in the new legislation, to oblige employees of Crown corporations to abide by the law. If they refuse to do so, they can just go work elsewhere. The least we can ask is that laws be clear, so that people stop feeling insecure like today.
I was just saying, Mr. Speaker, that we have found evidence in the services and I believe it was quite conclusive. I read an article this morning which proves once again how the CBC neglects, not to say despises, this appeal from the government. And just to quote one case, I have here an article published in La Presse of May 26 and written by Mr. Raymond Laplante, a consultant announcer for the CBC. I mention his name lest some ministers accuse him of being a separatist. Yet he is not a separatist; he merely pleads in favour of the French language. This announcer was returning from a trip to Vancouver. I quote what he says:
Last May 13, a Friday, defying all superstitions attached to that fatal date, I was aboard Air Canada flight 150 from Vancouver to Montreal. Except for a few clouds above the Rockies ...
-and so on. Further on he says:
Is there no one among your French-speaking customers who enjoys classical music? Do you think it would be too lofty for French Canadians?
Because all he heard on board was English, English songs, English music and all.
Once the classical music concert over, I switched to French songs, presented in French, naturally. But what a French! Something horrible with lot of nonsense at such a pace that you would need six hours more of flight to note them properly.
That is why he headlined his article, and I quote:
Lousy French at Air Canada. And that is not all! How many times during my numerous flights on Air Canada did I seethe inwardly on hearing some of your hostesses and stewards speak broken French in such a way you cannot even manage to decipher the message. What would happen during an emergency landing, when information has to be clear and precise, particularly in such situations where nervousness makes it more difficult to communicate?
That is the point I want to stress, Mr. Speaker. If CATCA and CALPA were making a plea against bilingualism, while we cannot even get a single word in French, what would happen in an emergency? That is what is called working towards safety.
Mr. Speaker, I will not read the whole article because it is rather long but I hope the remarks which were made about bilingualism have been noted and, as I said before, I want this question to be referred to committee, included in the legislation and made mandatory. Mechanics, hostesses and management should not forget that Air Canada is a Crown corporation and, as such, the property of a bilingual country. They must try to get used to the idea that Air Canada is owned by a bilingual country. We are all paying for it and we are glad to do so as long as it is providing good service to the whole population. This service must necessarily be bilingual.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose it is appropriate that we should be discussing this bill now as Air Canada enters its forty-first year of operations. Maybe after 40 years of operation it is time for any organization to be

May 27, 1977
Air Canada
reorganized, but I would have thought that the real reason for the existence of Air Canada or, as it was then called Trans-Canada Air Lines, was to provide a national air service for this country in the absence of any initiative by the private sector to provide such a service at the time.
Back in 1937 there was a great economic depression in the world and there was not a great deal of investment or development anywhere. I suppose there was clear justification for the establishment of a national air transportation service under the aegis of the Government of Canada at that time. I just regret that now, after 40 years of operation, many of which have been very successful, we are not moving toward a more independent type of operation which would give some incentive to this part of our air transport service to make a profit and to operate efficiently. This is a very important field of endeavour in Canada, and unfortunately, because of the way it has developed in the last number of years, it has not been particularly profitable for the people it is meant to serve. There have been examples of increasing deficits. We are being assured now that Air Canada is turning things around.
My friends in the New Democratic Party have suggested that losses have not been confined just to Air Canada but that other airlines have also suffered losses. They referred to the experience of Canadian Pacific Airline. I suggest that the reasons for the losses of Canadian Pacific are much different than the reasons for the losses sustained by Air Canada and relate primarily to the fact-which is a matter of government policy-that Canadian Pacific is restricted to 25 per cent of the available seats allotted to the national carrier, and Air Canada has the remaining 75 per cent. That puts Canadian Pacific at a disadvantage, and I personally think that the government should be trying to promote more competition with a view to making Air Canada more efficient and profitable rather than maintaining this protective mantle over Air Canada, as the government has done and seems to be persisting in doing.
Apart from that restriction we had the example last year of the bilateral routes. Canada obtained 20 new routes, 19 of which were assigned to Air Canada. I do not see any equity or any encouragement to Canadian Pacific there, and in my view that is one of the reasons why Canadian Pacific has not been doing very well recently. In particular, Canadian Pacific made a big investment in the west coast traffic to San Francisco and California generally. It developed that traffic, but what happened when these bilateral agreements were entered into? Air Canada was assigned new routes into California at the expense of Canadian Pacific. I think that was a very unjust and inequitable way for the Government of Canada to proceed.
Nevertheless, we are faced with Bill C-17, which is supposed to re-organize Air Canada and put it on a more businesslike and efficient footing. The bill affects all the major air carriers in Canada, but in particular it affects the protected flag carrier, Air Canada. Because it affects more than one carrier, I think something should be said about the Canadian air

industry in general. In 1975 commercial air carriers in Canada transported more than 20 million passengers. That came very close to moving the entire population of this country, and that only serves to point up the cardinal importance of air travel in Canada. In addition to that, three million travellers arrived in Canada by air from abroad. After having paid their air fares they spent half a billion dollars here. That accounts for a significant contribution toward a net gain in the economy of Canada.
On the whole, air travel has grown safer, faster, and more efficient. It has tried to maintain reasonable fares when the cost of living has continued to increase. It has reached out to serve isolated communities. It crosses oceans and continents in a matter of hours. However, there is a real fear that current government policies are severely damaging the industry. We hear a great many complaints about service and about delays in air travel. In our own travels to and from our constituencies we experience such annoyances and inconveniences ourselves. We certainly do not like being subjected to these situations, and we can fully understand and appreciate the feelings of vast numbers of other Canadians who complain about the inefficiency of the operations of Air Canada. Of course Air Canada tends to take the brunt of this because, as I pointed out, it is allotted 75 per cent of the transcontinental business through government policy.
In 1975 Canadian air carriers lost $18.8 million. Regional air carriers lost more than $750,000. It seems to me, from the information I have, that Air Canada's losses have been higher than any of the other carriers. The explanations of Air Canada have never satisfied me. Air Canada has been able to obtain the best routes. It has left the short hops and short hauls to the regional carriers, but nevertheless the regional carriers seem to be able to make a better go of this small potatoes type of business than Air Canada can with the cream of the crop.
It is quite clear that something needs to be done. The basic question is whether this bill will accomplish anything. In the ten years prior to 1975, that is, from 1965 up to 1974, air revenues increased four times. But net income fell to less than half, while the number of passengers carried increased three times, and revenue per mile went up three and one-half times. At the same time operating costs went up four times and wages doubled. However, there appears to be some hope.
The Ministry of Transport now says that no more airports will be built without the airlines being consulted first. That is a very refreshing attitude, and it is nice to see some common sense being injected into the operations of the government. I just wonder what would have happened to Mirabel if the airlines had been consulted in any way, shape or form about the construction of that massive boondoggle which was, in my view, built strictly for political reasons at the expense of the whole economy. They probably will turn out to be the wrong political reasons, and it is likely that nobody will be satisfied with what has happened there. Thank goodness the political situation which developed two or three years ago stopped a similar thing happening at Pickering, and we hope that the
May 27, 1977

new found reason of the Ministry of Transport in consulting the major users of these facilities will be lasting.
In the case of the airport at Calgary it looks as though we are going to have a wonderful facility. The difficulty is that as a result of design costs which have been built into it-which are the complete responsibility of the Ministry of Transport- most of the prospective users of that facility are unsure whether they will be able to utilize the facility at the cost being mentioned by the Ministry of Transport.
The key to operating any business successfully is profit, and I think that certainly should apply to Crown corporations as well as to any other type of corporation. Unfortunately Crown corporations seem to be insulated from that imperative more than corporations funded by individuals with their own money. Profit is important to any airline because of the cost of replacing aircraft, among other things. In 1970 a Boeing 747 cost $24 million. In a couple of years from now the same aircraft will cost between $45 million and $50 million. I must ask whether this bill will allow Air Canada to make a profit more readily, or if it will further hamper the airlines money making efforts.
I think at this stage we should look at some of the provisions of the bill. The most significant proposals are, first, authorization for Air Canada to engage in a wider range of activities; second, ownership would pass from the CNR directly to the government; third, the amount of authorized capital stock would be increased; and fourth, Air Canada would be permitted to seek debt financing in the market place and not be compelled to apply to the government for any future financing.
With respect to broader powers, Air Canada is rather restricted by the terms of the present act in the type of activities in which it can engage. The proposed act broadens the "capacities and activities" which the company may undertake, both within and outside Canada. Aside from operating the business of an air carrier, there are references to hotels and other accommodation; surface vehicles and facilities for the transportation and housing of persons, goods and mail; services, facilities and equipment for organizing and conducting tours; catering and providing other passenger-related services, including reservations for transportation and accommodation, computer and tele-processing systems, and technical, advisory and consulting services. Furthermore, the new act permits the company to establish or invest in subsidiary companies, provided authorization of the governor in council is first obtained.
On the question of ownership it will be noted that up to the present Air Canada's capital stock has always been held by the CNR-itself a Crown corporation-which meant that Air Canada was in effect a CN wholly-owned subsidiary. As shareholder, the CN was authorized to appoint five members to the Air Canada board of directors, while the governor in council appointed four. Of course cabinet appointed the board of directors of CN so it was pretty well able to control the appointment of all directors. The proposed act stipulates that shares of Air Canada will be held by the Minister of Transport
Air Canada
"in trust for Her Majesty in right of Canada", and that shares are not transferable. It further provides that the corporation will be under the management of a board of directors comprised of the chairman and the president and not more than 13 other directors, all of whom are appointed by the governor in council.
I think the words "governor in council" are the key to this bill and the dilemma in which the government finds itself. On the one hand it wants an airline operation that is set up under the guise of a Crown corporation and which should have some degree of independence. Because of the history of bad management in Air Canada, however, largely as a result of actions of people the government itself appointed to run the corporation, it did not want to give it too much authority to act on its own. On the face of it the bill gives Air Canada broad powers, but like so many Liberal ideas, appearances are deceiving. While it appears the reorganized company can do almost anything, the hooker in this situation is that nothing can be done without the approval of the governor in council.
As the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) pointed, out, Air Canada which is supposed to be an independent Crown corporation, cannot even appoint auditors without the approval of cabinet. As far as auditors are concerned I think all Crown corporations should be subject to audit by the Auditor General of Canada. I do not want to slander the auditing profession of this country, but I have seen some rather strange certificates issued by auditors of government agencies and Crown corporations. I suggest the reason they are strange is that the auditors want to hold the accounts. We need a truly independent auditing service of government agencies if we are to get the best value for our dollar. I think it is very strange indeed that the government can use the appointment of auditors as patronage. That should not be involved with Crown corporations.
When this bill goes to committee I hope very serious consideration will be given to the appointment of the Auditor General of Canada as auditor of this organization.
I believe that Air Canada is being transformed into an agency of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang); it is going to join his fiefdom. This bill is not a step toward making the corporation compatible with normal commercial enterprise as should be done. I think the philosophy of this bill and the reason why so many possible objects of the corporation have been listed, is that anything that is not listed is totally beyond the power of the corporation. In itself that is a restriction on the flexibility the government says it is trying to give Air Canada in the management of its day-to-day affairs but, because of what is being done here making Air Canada an agency of the government, we are to have continuing troubles with language.
The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), who spoke before me, complained that Air Canada was not living up to the requirements of the government's bilingual program. I think part of the cause of the sense of alienation that has developed in the west is the fact that Francophone cabin crews-which the hon. member says are inadequate for use in

May 27, 1977
Air Canada
Quebec-are operating there. A lot of passengers complain of inadequate service because the crews do not understand English very well. That shows a lack of flexibility, or a breakdown of some kind. We find crews who cannot understand French operating in Quebec and ones who cannot understand English operating out west. It is not a good situation. I do not think the company's being closely identified with the government in its day-to-day operations will help the situation.
I use this opportunity to complain about the procurement policy of Air Canada, particularly with regard to meat. When I asked back in 1971 why Air Canada was not using Canadian beef exclusively for in-flight meals, I was told there was not enough to go around. That answer was not satisfactory then, and is even less satisfactory now, considering what our livestock industry has been through in the last three years and its present state.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a distinct possibility that we may become involved in a debate this afternoon.
