subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Heaven forbid that we should so spoil the tranquillity of a Friday afternoon in this House, the afternoon of the most productive day of the week. I hope hon. members will pay their usual, studied attention to the remarks I am about to make.
I will take advantage of the opportunity afforded by the debate on Bill C-17 to raise some questions about Air Canada and the service our national air carrier provides in my part of the country. It is appropriate that I should do so because we are considering what will probably be the most fundamental change affecting Air Canada since its founding 40 years ago.
I find that my position is somewhat different from that adopted by some of my colleagues. I come from a part of the country in which Air Canada enjoys a virtual monopoly in air transport. Consequently the provisions of this bill which would make the airline more accountable to government and hence parliament are all the more meaningful and relevant.
It has been somewhat difficult to raise questions in the House about Air Canada and the quality of Air Canada service, because of the ambiguity of Air Canada's position vis-a-vis the government and its parent Crown corporation, Canadian National Railways. Given the inflation which has overtaken our economy and the higher price of fuel, it is true

May 27, 1977

to say that air travel is being restricted to fewer and fewer people. Unless the government recognizes soon the importance of Air Canada and of air travel in this country, only members of parliament, senior civil servants, and businessmen on expenses allowances will be able to fly.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
That may be all very well in the corridor regions of central and western Canada where, because economies are buoyant, people can afford air travel. But the situation is somewhat different in my part of the country. Many people of my area depend almost exclusively on aircraft for travel to Montreal, Ottawa or Toronto. The hardships and restrictions arising from the present situation should therefore be obvious.
The crisis in energy prices is affecting the attitude of the airlines. I suppose one can hardly blame Air Canada for its attitude. It must pay the same inflated price for fuel and the same wages as its competitors must pay. Consequently the company has sought to reduce the number of its less profitable runs. That policy has reduced the frequency of air service available to people resident in my constituency. As I said, for many of my constituents Air Canada proves to be the only efficient way of travel to other centres of this country. Let me demonstrate what I mean.
Last year we were served by an L-1011. Because of the large number of empty seats on the flight, I felt the use of such equipment was not justified. That aircraft was supported by three DC-9s and one DC-8. That provided adequate service. Indeed, as a result of the L-1011 there was a surplus of seats. I knew this situation would not be tolerated for long. I made the point before hearings of the CTC on regional air transport that we did not want the big equipment, that the L-101 Is could be taken off and replaced by DC-9s-in other words, increase the flight frequency. This would result in increased economy in terms of utilization of seat capacity because more flights would be available throughout the day. That situation merely resulted in the present schedules. We have no L-1011. The number of flights has been reduced even further to the point at which, at the present time, we have only four flights. This has to be viewed with concern.
I began my remarks by saying I supported in the main the principle of this bill which, it seems to me, would make Air Canada more accountable to parliament and give us a better opportunity to monitor these arbitrary changes which are made from time to time by Air Canada in the interests of economy. After all, the people who depend on Air Canada, since it enjoys a monopoly position, are the ones who bear the burden of these economies.
I should like to lay before the Elouse the situation which prevails at the present time. There are no direct flights from St. John's though it has a catchment area of approximately 250,000 people. Air Canada is the only national carrier coming in there apart from the regional carrier about which I
Air Canada
shall have more to say later. Air Canada has no competition on this run from St. John's to Elalifax, Montreal and Toronto.
In the past we always enjoyed the privilege of a direct flight to Montreal. Now we have to go through Halifax, sometimes necessitating expensive stop-overs. On Saturdays there is only one flight to Montreal even via Halifax, so the situation at weekends is even worse than it is during the week. There is now only one direct flight to Toronto. Here is a market which depends solely on Air Canada.
My hon. friend made reference to EPA. EPA does not at this moment enjoy the right to carry traffic direct from St. John's through Halifax to Montreal. If it did, that would constitute a different situation entirely. Pending before the CTC at the present time is an application to provide such a service. Should it be granted, there would be some element of competition, and I submit it would result in some improvement in the service. The present service provided by Air Canada shows a marked deterioration the further east one gets. By the time it reaches my part of the country the service has deteriorated considerably.
If the CTC rules favourably on this application the situation will be changed not only in terms of better service but in terms of the financial viability of our regional carrier, Eastern Provincial Airways. This is a matter which is of vital importance because EPA has to cope with the same conditions as other airlines when it comes to equipment, fuel supplies, and personnel. Under its licensing conditions it has to provide service on uneconomic runs within the region, and unless it has access to profitable runs to offset the losses incurred, something obviously has to go. Either the service goes or flight frequency has to be reduced. In any case, the travelling public is the loser.
I can understand the importance of utilizing the substantial facilities which now exist at Halifax International Airport but I submit that a market with a catchment of 250,000 is sufficient, especially at this time of the year, to warrant special consideration. Why cannot we have a direct flight from St. John's to Montreal? Why cannot there be a direct flight from St. John's to the national capital, terminating in Toronto? We are the only major city in the country, indeed the only provincial capital in this part of the country, which does not have a direct service to the nation's capital. As I see it, there is not likely to be any substantial improvement. We will get an extra flight as of the latter part of June and this is supposed to handle a volume of traffic which is increasing annually as tourism grows.
In all this we have to consider the increasing importance of St. John's as a convention centre. This year a number of major national conventions are taking place in our city in addition to the Canada Summer Games. This is bound to mean a substantial increase in tourist traffic.
I take advantage of the second reading of this bill to put forward these complaints. I could spend time talking about the cancelled flights for which the excuse of adverse weather forecasts is given. Later it usually turns out that the flights had been cancelled because, in the opinion of dispatchers in Montreal, there was not enough traffic to warrant putting in
6030

May 27, 1977
Air Canada
the equipment. So the 15 or 20 people who have booked flights and who are depending on Air Canada are suddenly stranded. This happens frequently. I know it happens. I have established beyond any doubt that it happens, but I cannot prove it. Moreover, 1 have no means of redress open to me because the annual Air Canada report no longer comes before the Transport Committee as used to be the case.
I hope that some of the measures being taken in the bill will make the airline more accountable to the representatives of the Canadian people because, after all, we are in the position of being shareholders. It is our airline and it ought to be accountable to us.
Reference has been made to the provisions having to do with the board of directors. I should like to see some statutory term set for these directorships to give the directors greater independence and greater ability to respond to the needs of the airline while at the same time remaining accountable to parliament. This raises a question which was touched on by my hon. friend who just resumed his seat.
It is proposed to change the structure of Air Canada in such a way as to make it a separate Crown agency. I would draw the government's attention to the recommendation of the Auditor General with regard to the auditing of accounts of Crown corporations. Last year the airline got into difficulties over illegalities in connection with its transactions with a travel agency. As a result of some of the measures proposed in this bill, Air Canada will now be able to engage in necessary transactions of this kind without resorting to the methods which came under such criticism earlier. But if Air Canada were accountable to the House financially through the Auditor General it would be an even greater safeguard.
Getting back to the board of directors, I should like to see some kind of statutory term for people appointed to represent the interests of the taxpayer. I should like to see some account taken of regional representation, not in terms of one representative on the board for the Atlantic provinces but representatives of peak traffic areas where the airline is vitally important as the single carrier. For example, there is no other way at the present time out of my province, unless one wants to hazard a 600 mile drive along the trans-Newfoundland portion of the trans-Canada highway and then cross the Gulf of St. Lawrence, which takes at least two days, than to use Air Canada. I believe that representation on the board should take into account this kind of regional situation. Each province should be represented on the board of directors instead of one individual representing the interests of all of the Atlantic provinces, including the Gaspe region of Quebec, and several members representing central Canadian provinces like Ontario.
I could go on to outline the complaints I have received. Not a month goes by when a complaint does not come over my desk about the quality of service of Air Canada in my constituency. But I must say this about Mr. Taylor, the new president of Air Canada. I have noted a much more receptive attitude to

complaints. In his responses I have noted a much more positive approach to customer complaints raised through members of parliament. I congratulate him on the excellent job he seems to be doing. He has certainly succeeded in restoring morale, which had sunk to an all time low and which itself seriously adversely affected quality of service. I believe it was an enlightened appointment by the government of a man who had worked his way up through Air Canada from ticket agent to the top. He understands the people who work within the airline, and as well has had direct experience of dealing with people over the counter. He understands the problems encountered on a day to day basis by the travelling public.
With his comprehensive experience we have at the head of our national airline a man who is able to make a positive response to problems and to handle them in a most constructive way. I believe he has brought about a 1,000 per cent improvement over the former ambivalent situation where the chairman of the board had executive authority and the president of the company had administrative authority and you did not know with whom you were dealing. Not only that, but middle management and the operating personnel were having difficulty over what the line of command was within the airline.
I look forward to this bill proceeding to committee and to the government providing us with explanations as to what exactly is intended by some of its provisions, especially with regard to the appointment of directors. I should like to know what are the intentions of the government with respect to establishment of schedules and timetables. Surely the public has a right to give some input to the scheduling of Air Canada, although not so much in competitive situations because there the competitive factor has to be uppermost. The company must be allowed to compete on an equal basis with the private commercial carriers. But in areas where Air Canada enjoys a monopoly, of which there are a number, including my own province, the public should express its views through various organizations such as boards of trade and chambers of commerce. Air Canada can also hear what the public has to say by coming to parliament every year. There should be this kind of conduit, if you like, to provide direct public input into the scheduling of the airline.
With those few words 1 look forward to the bill going to committee and to hearing from the minister. I look forward to hearing what the transportation committee will encounter as it visits the Atlantic provinces. It begins to tour the Atlantic provinces on Sunday, and one of the areas it will look into is the role of regional airports and regional air traffic within the Atlantic provinces. This is something which has a direct bearing on Atlantic Canada because it raises the whole question of a regional air policy, one which will make it possible for regional air carriers to continue.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF DISHONOURED CHEQUES
speechtext:
1 would not want to cut into the livelihood of anyone in that noble profession, but it does seem to me that the clause under consideration, in its application and its operation if not in its wording, puts businessmen and merchants, in particular, through a great deal of unnecessary legal expense in order to recover payment for bad cheques.
It may seem that nothing could be more satisfactory than the law as it is presently worded. At present there is a presumption the accused has obtained something of value by false pretence, if he has passed an NSF cheque, unless the court is satisfied by evidence indicating when the accused issued the cheque he had reasonable grounds to believe that it would be honoured, if presented for payment within a reasonable time after it was issued. It seems to say that there is a presumption of intent to defraud whenever an NSF cheque is written. The law places the onus squarely on the accused to prove his NSF cheque is not what it appears to be and that there was no attempt to obtain something of value by false pretence.
Let us admit there are a good many reasons for writing a bad cheque. In cases of honest error, the maker or drawer, as he is called in the banking trade, will redeem his worthless cheque promptly, after having been notified that his cheque was dishonoured. Payment in such cases, or even arrangement to pay, is sufficient evidence to indicate the cheque drawer did not intend fraud, as it might otherwise appear.
Even if this allows the drawer the benefit of a large doubt in many cases, all the merchant wants is the payment he thought he had received in the first place. Truthfully, payment is the only completely satisfactory evidence that there was no intent to defraud. According to the wording of the present law, although the bad cheque writer is required to prove he thought his cheque would be honoured, he is not required to honour his cheque in order to satisfy the courts his intentions were honourable. In practice, and quite contrary to the wording of the existing law, the prosecution is required to prove the drawer obtained his goods under false pretence. Experience has shown chances for the prosecution to obtain a conviction are quite slim, I suppose because fraud is rightly considered a serious offence and the courts would rather err on the side of the accused.
In its operation the present law is so inequitable it sometimes seems even to conspire with other laws against the honest businessman, as in the case of a landlord who recently complained he was unable to obtain the assistance of police in prosecuting a tenant for fraud, even though the tenant had issued not one but several NSF cheques for rent which was now in arrears. The police explained the tenant's location was known to the landlord, with whom he was in a contractual relationship. There could, therefore, be no criminal offence. The tenant felt secure under Ontario's Landlord and Tenant
Act, at least until spring. The courts would rather look upon this tenant as a bad debtor and assume that writing NSF cheques for rent is just another way of not paying the rent on time.
The landlord in this case did not specify whether the cheques were postdated. If they were, I might agree with the courts in preferring to look upon this as a bad debt. It ought to be made clear a bad cheque is not the same as a bad debt when it is written and delivered, that is to say, issued by the drawer in payment for something of value, whether to buy a camera, a car, or to pay the rent.
I do not have to remind hon. members present that a personal cheque, like a bank note or dollar, is a piece of commercial paper, payable at sight or at the time it is presented for payment by the payee. Like the bank note, it is issued on the faith that there are funds to cover it; but unlike the bank note it is not legal tender and does not have to be accepted by a businessman. The personal cheque is a convenience and a protection to the consumer, but under the operation of the present law against cheque frauds it is nothing but an expensive risk to the merchant. When a merchant accepts a personal cheque, he does not intend to extend credit. He is not expecting payment at some future date. He accepts a personal cheque as a substitute for cash, usually banks the cheque with his cash the same day, and immediately receives payment from his bank.
When a cheque is returned to the merchant because of insufficient funds, it is charged back to him, and only then does he discover that, contrary to his expectation, it was not a cash sale. If the personal cheque he accepted represents a line of credit to his customer, or some vague promise to pay, the merchant could at least have verified the credit standing of his customer so as to determine the likelihood of his ability to pay, given the status of his present obligations and the record of his credit dealings in the past, not to mention his income. Instead, the merchant asks for identification, considering quite rightly his principal obligation at the time of sale is to verify his customer is whoever he says he is. After all, the law does presume an intent to defraud on the basis of an NSF cheque. This should inspire the merchant to have some confidence in the personal cheque as an alternative to cash payment.
As we have seen, the operation of the law does not live up to its wording. One of the inevitable results is that personal cheques are being refused everywhere by merchants who have been disillusioned by a law which does not mean what it says. When someone passes counterfeit bank notes for cash, not even restitution will save him from the slammer. When a customer deliberately passes an NSF cheque, a counterfeit cheque in other words, restitution or payment is not even required in order to show good faith and to clear him of the presumption of false pretence, which the law says his worthless cheque represents.
What kind of justice is this when the merchant must take all the risk; when the law requires nothing from the cheque counterfeiter by way of payment, but prefers to look only at his bank account and his circumstances in order to determine

May 27, 1977

his guilt or innocence of fraud; when the merchant must then assume the cost of civil prosecution in what is most often a fruitless effort to recover payment for something of value, which the court thinks of as a debt, as though the merchant had somehow extended credit at the time of purchase? Having stolen the merchandise in the first place, the white collar thief is then confirmed in possession of his goods by the frequent misapplication of law by the courts which prefer to call the thief a borrower. Shoplifting may now be considered theft, but pay for your groceries with a worthless cheque and the courts will call you a bad debtor.
The advantages of writing a bum cheque are nowhere more striking than in the application of the present law whereby the cheque counterfeiter is, in practice and in contradiction of the evidence which his rubber cheque provides, presumed innocent until proven guilty of doing it deliberately. The criminal law offers no satisfaction to the merchant. It does not provide for repayment, nor does it deter others from committing the same kind of crime.
According to Sgt. Lewis Coray of the London police department, fraud division, one of the reasons for the 150 per cent increase in bank frauds since 1972 is the lack of risk in committing white collar crimes. Sergeant Coray agreed with a number of other participants at a recent seminar on fraud, sponsored by the Canadian Banker's Association, who found the courts at fault in not imposing fair sentences on the relatively few who are convicted of fraud. Cheque thieves, he said, too often "Get off with a slap on the wrist."
When a cheque thief is convicted and sentenced for his fraud, the crime is usually spectacular, and the conviction makes headlines, as it did in the London Free Press of February 3 this year, when one woman, unable to make restitution for 53 bad cheques, amounting to almost $5,000, was reported to have been given an indeterminate sentence not to exceed 18 months. Perhaps she has learned the lessons of successful cheque fraud. Keep the number of your bad cheques, and the individual amounts, to a minimum so that the courts will not feel obliged to slap your wrists and the merchant cannot afford to sue.
In passing sentence on this woman, the judge said:
It's no wonder law-abiding citizens encounter problems when they try to write a cheque. The stores have been taken already by too many persons like yourself.
But despite her conviction, any stranger who has spent much of his time reading our criminal court records would come away with the impression that Canadians, while rarely found guilty of fraud, are plagued with an abundance of bad bookkeepers.
There is no need to ask: what is the effect of the increase of cheque fraud on the use of personal cheques? The acceptance of personal cheques depends not so much on the credit of the issuer as on the confidence of the businessman in the value of the paper he is offered. Because there is so little risk involved in writing bad cheques, and also because the cheque counterfeiter knows he will not have to pay up in order to avoid
Criminal Code
conviction for false pretence, business confidence in personal cheques has been so badly eroded under our existing law that this type of commercial paper-the only ready substitute for cash-faces extinction as a method of payment for goods purchased.
The merchant who accepts a personal cheque-even from a known customer-is becoming as rare as the corner grocer who accepts telephone orders and lets you charge them.
The only alternative to cash for consumers is the credit card. The risk of this form of credit is assumed by the bank or department store which issues the card, and the cost of that risk is paid by us all, whether we use such a card or pay cash. Nor has the merchant been slow to see the advantage of Chargex and Mastercharge. He has learned that credit customers buy 33 per cent more than cash customers because credit customers, unlike those who write personal cheques, are not compelled to determine whether or not they can cover the cost of the purchase from available funds. Credit customers are merely mortgaging their future income.
For the sake of counterfeit cheque writers, therefore, we are forcing the ordinary consumer to purchase on credit, to become a debtor, and too often a bad debtor who gets in over his head. Is this what we want, or are we prepared to put some teeth into the present law against cheque frauds before cheques disappear altogether?
Cheque counterfeiters in this country should be grateful for having been born in Canada. In France, cheque fraud is a little more risky. French law treats the NSF cheque as an offence. The severity of punishment depends on the amount of money involved, but the fraud is considered serious if the NSF cheque amounts to $200 or more. The convicted person becomes subject to a penalty of one to five years in jail, and a fine of $720 to $7,200.
But, no matter what the amount of the cheque, the elements of the offence are the same: first, issuance of the cheque, which excludes post-dated cheques; second, lack of funds at the moment of issue; and, third, bad faith of the author of the cheque.
And just what is bad faith, you might ask? Bad faith does not suppose even the intention to cheat or defraud. It does not necessarily mean that the person who wrote the cheque knew there were insufficient funds. French courts assume that a person writing a cheque has the duty of knowing the state of his account and, therefore, bad faith may be proven in the case of a person who, in doubt of his situation, writes a cheque without taking the precaution of verifying the state of his account. I do not think that is too hard to accept.
If the amount involved is less than $200, the offence is considered a breach of regulations. Not only is the punishment less severe, but the bad cheque speaks for the bad faith of the author of the cheque, and off he goes to jail for writing a cheque without checking his balance.
I understand that penal legislation concerning cheques was temporarily altered in 1972 because the courts were clogged with NSF'ers waiting for their turn in the pokey. Since then,

May 27, 1977
Criminal Code
at least until last year, in order to clear up the backlog, a period of ten days was allowed the author of the bad cheque from the time of the issuance of the cheque during which he could make the repayment. The person who paid up was able to escape jail but was still liable to the payment of a fine.
By contrast, the present bill allows the cheque counterfeiter and bad bookkeeper alike 30 days to pay what they owe as evidence that they did not obtain something of value under false pretence. Anyone who thinks this to be too harsh should state why a Canadian crook deserves to be treated better than a French thief.
For the sake of every consumer in the market place and every merchant with whom he deals, I cannot urge too strongly upon the members of this House the need for a simple and effective law which would identify and eliminate the cheque counterfeiter by prosecution by the Crown without requiring the merchant to weigh the cost and the benefit of trying to collect payment for bad cheques. In my view, the proposed bill will provide such a law and I heartily recommend its passage.
Mir. Walter Baker (Grenville-Carleton): Mr. Speaker, I listened with an abiding interest to the hon. member who has just spoken and put forward this bill on behalf of the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner). Because of the high position which the hon. member for London East holds in the House he is prohibited from presenting bills, and I understand that is the reason why he did not do it himself.
I want to commend the hon. member for Middlesex-Lon-don-Lambton (Mr. Condon) as a non-lawyer, as he identified himself, for the presentation which he made. If I should disagree with some of the things he said, I do not want him to feel that I am disagreeing in any way with the motivation behind the bill because it is indeed true in this country that we have to find a method of dealing with the increasing incidence of bad cheque writing and a whole host of other things that have afflicted me and other members of the House, and indeed, and in particular, business people throughout the country. We have to find that way. Listening to the hon. member elucidate on the problem-and I agree with the ramifications and the extent of the problem-I had to ask myself whether this was the way and whether we ought to depart from a principle of justice in Canada to meet a problem which we might be able to meet in another way.
The existing law as contained in the Criminal Code and as set forth in the fly sheet of the bill reads this way:
Where ... it is shown that anything was obtained by the accused by means of a cheque that, when presented for payment within a reasonable time, was dishonoured on the ground that no funds or insufficient funds were on deposit to the credit of the accused in the bank or other institution on which the cheque was drawn, it shall be presumed-
That is the law at the moment, a presumption.
-to have been obtained by a false pretence-
There is a presumption now existing in the law of a false pretence, and if the accused who has drawn the cheque cannot rebut that presumption, then certain consequences flow.

The Criminal Code then goes on to say:
-unless the court is satisfied by evidence that when the accused issued the cheque he had reasonable grounds to believe that it would be honoured if presented for payment within a reasonable time after it was issued.
The court is instructed to look into the mind of the issuer of the cheque, to consider the time of presentation and to consider the accused's circumstances. The bill which is proposed and which has been discussed in an able way by the hon. member who just sat down, changes the conditions. The proposed amendment would repeal the section, but it reads the same until it gets down to these words:
.. . unless the accused pays the amount of the dishonoured cheque to the payee thereof within thirty days after the bank or other institution on which the cheque was drawn notifies the accused by prepaid mail that the cheque was dishonoured.
If we stop to think about it for a moment, there is an element in this proposal which I do not think is intended by the drafter of the bill. The element is that it really allows 30 days' credit which could be used by the unscrupulous in a way in which I am sure the hon. member for London East never intended when he prepared the bill. A person could write a cheque knowing full well that his account had no money in it and would not have any money in it within a period of 30 days, and that cheque could be honoured.
What this bill really does is establish in the Criminal Code a rather unique line of credit, and what is lost is the opportunity for an accusation to be made, and information to be issued, and a person to be tried, whether or not the cheque is paid later on. As the section now exists it says that if anybody tries to use the existence of the Criminal Code to give himself a line of credit by issuing bum cheques, even though he should pay those cheques before he comes to trial, he is still guilty of an offence. He is subject to be examined with respect to that, and the circumstances of paying the cheques go only to the mitigation of sentence, but they do not take away from the case, at least at this point, the sanction of a penalty. I do not think the hon. member for London East intended that, but that could well be the effect of his bill.
I do not want hon. members to think that by saying that I am unmindful of the problems of business people, but I am also not unmindful of the problems of some people in the community. I carry no brief for the fraud artist, but I am prepared to carry a brief for people who are accidentally caught within the provisions of the Criminal Code. This has happened under this section, and it has happened within my experience.
A few years ago I was asked to defend a man who was engaged in a plumbing business and who subsequently went bankrupt. This person issued a series of cheques. For some reason or other some cheques were presented in time and were paid. One cheque, I suppose because of the negligence of the person to whom it was directed, the payee, was not presented in time, and when it was presented there were not sufficient funds in the bank because of the difficulties into which my client had got himself. Under the bill as proposed a person like this would have 30 days to raise sufficient money to pay the cheques, but in my client's circumstances there was no way on
May 27, 1977

God's green earth that he would ever be able to raise the money.
This man was not a dishonest man. He was a foolish businessman, but he was not fraudulent. He did not try to conceal or withhold. He was married. He had two children. He lost his car, his home, and everything he owned as a result of this, but he was not dishonest. He was unfortunate, but had the bill which is being presented today for the approval of this House been the law of the land, this man would have been branded a criminal merely because he could not pay. He would not have had a chance to defend himself against a charge of criminality.
As a result of these circumstances we appeared before a magistrate, I think it was, in the city of Cornwall, which is represented by the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley). We now call magistrates provincial judges. We advanced evidence at that time of the state of my client's bank account, his circumstances and the circumstances of his business, and we were able on that occasion to rebut the presumption which is set forth in the Criminal Code, the presumption that he issued the cheque knowing that it would not be honoured. The court found that this fellow had issued a bad cheque, that he had obtained goods on the basis of a bad cheque but that he did not do it on false pretences.
If that poor fellow had been found guilty, he would have been fined, and if he could not pay the fine, he would have spent time in jail. We would have resurrected, had this bill been the law of the land, the old debtor's prison. 1 know there are some businessmen in the country who would like there to be debtor's prisons. It would be a great place. That in effect is what would happen in a case like this, and I do not think my case is unique. My practice was never unique. These cases came up time and time again. The businessman is as much inconvenienced by cheque-bouncing artists as he is by the innocent, I suppose, but I think it is our duty with respect to the criminal law to ensure that it is administered in such a way that the truly innocent do not suffer, and that is the matter which concerns me about this bill.
The other thing about cheques is that they involve an element of volition. Cheques are volunteered by people who issue them, and they are accepted. When cheques are used, there is a certain amount of risk which a businessman has to take. That is why, as the hon. member said, a cheque is a different kind of instrument. That is the reason why I think the bill ought not to be supported. 1 say that with some regret because 1 know the motivation of the hon. member who advanced the bill, and I listened with great care to the hon. member who presented it for him. If the bill were approved I think it would bring something into our criminal administration that was taken out of it many years ago, and for good reason.
The courts of the country are equipped to look into these matters. Appointments to provincial courts in all the provinces are made with great care. Those are the courts that usually
Criminal Code
deal with this kind of matter and I think we should trust them.
I am not going to argue that the lists are not crowded, because they are; cases take some time to be heard, but it is within the hand and mind of man to change the procedures, to appoint more judges, or do a host of other things that would help the situation. I do not think we ought to undo an inconvenience by removing from our criminal justice system a protection that has been built in over a period of time for good reason.
There are two elements to consider in this matter. There is the element represented by the businessman who is angry because his goods have gone and all he has for them is a rubber cheque. But there is also the other aspect, the element of innocence. If anyone in our community, when he faces a presumption of guilt, does not have the opportunity to prove himself innocent, not just so that somebody gets paid but because of his own reputation in the community, his standing in his family, or his view of himself-if that is removed from the Criminal Code then I think it would be a tragedy. I do not think the hon. member for London East intended that by his bill, but unfortunately that is the effect of it. I therefore say with some regret that I do not believe the bill ought to be supported in its present condition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to commend the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) for presenting this bill, as I have great respect and friendship for him. I appreciate his concern with regard to the passing of bad cheques.
I should like to direct my attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon) who made an able presentation. He said that in London there has been an increase of 150 per cent in bad cheques passed since 1972. Mr. Speaker, you do not have to be too old to appreciate that at one time we had a cash society; everything was paid for in cash, and some of our parents adhere to that principle. Unless they can pay cash for goods they do not buy them. The second phase was cash plus cheque, and the third phase, which we are now experiencing, is cash plus cheque plus credit card.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) was at one time a Crown attorney in Ottawa. He knows as well as I, from my experience in criminal law, that the police are wary of laying a charge with regard to a cheque. Once the Crown authorities assume responsibility with regard to such a charge they may be exposing themselves to an action for false prosecution. My experience in Toronto was that Crown counsel were very reluctant to proceed with regard to cheques. They quite rightly said it was not a criminal matter but a civil matter, and advised the person who received the bad cheque to use civil proceedings.
The hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton said that the nub of the matter is that the person who received the bad cheque wants payment for the goods or services. We have therefore to determine whether the amendment would achieve that purpose. Mr. Speaker, I feel it will not achieve the purpose the hon. member seeks. It does not help the ordinary businessman to tighten the criminal law, and it does not help

May 27, 1977
Criminal Code
the ordinary person who receives a cheque for rent, say, to bring an action in the criminal courts. What will happen is not that the payment will be made to the person who received the bad cheque but that a penalty or prison sentence may be imposed on the person who passed it.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton picked up an important point very quickly when he said the effect of this bill will be to extend free credit for at least 30 days to the person who passes the cheque. In other words, that person would have 30 days in which to honour it; if he does that, then the case is at an end. He would not only have credit for 30 days but, according to the bill, for 30 days plus the time the bank took to notify him.
You can appreciate some of the things that could happen, Mr. Speaker. Someone could think he has certain moneys in the bank, present a cheque for payment for goods and services, and then go away on a month's holiday or be confined to hospital. This might far exceed the 30 days and the presumption of false pretences would arise immediately. I do not think most of us want this. What we want is what the hon. member who introduced the bill said: we want payment. I think we have to find ways and means of getting moneys to the person who accepted the cheque.
Again I give full credit to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton for saying there is a certain risk when a cheque is presented as payment for goods or services. The person who accepts it has to be very careful about the person who presents it. At times people are foolish about accepting cheques and they have to accept the consequences. They have to accept that they should take action in the ordinary way through the civil court to receive their money. I do not think the criminal court should be cluttered with cases of false pretences concerning small cheques.
Once a person gets a criminal conviction it is very difficult to expunge it. This would impose a very heavy burden on a person who did not pay within the 30 days or the 30 days plus the time it took the bank to inform him.
That does not mean we should not study this matter. It seems to me that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) should pick up this idea with regard to bad cheques and refer it to the Law Reform Commission for study, or to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, where bank officials and consumer associations, police, lawyers and others could be called for an opinion.
I could not help but smile when the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton presented the bill and said that it may deny lawyers some form of income. The average lawyer thinks these cases a nuisance and makes little money from them as I am sure my colleagues, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, and the hon. member for Toronto-Lake-shore (Mr. Robinson) will agree.

Although the proposed change in the law would lead to no great loss of income for lawyers, it would not solve the problem confronting us. We must consider ways and means to adopt the principle on which the mover of the bill spoke, the principle of repayment of bad cheques. It seems to me that the present law is preferable to the proposed amendment.
At present the law says that the accused must show he had reasonable grounds for believing that if the cheque were presented within a reasonable time after issue it would be honoured. But the amendment would impose a time frame, and the time frame would give the cheque writer extended credit for 30 days, plus the time it takes the bank to notify the issuer of the cheque. Although I have deep respect and affection for the hon. member for London East and was pleased to hear the presentation of the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton, I cannot accept the proposed amendment in its present form, and I hope the Minister of Justice will refer this question to the Law Reform Commission for study.
In law, there are federal cases and civil cases, for the most part, and in law presumption is a rarely invoked principle. In a criminal case the onus is almost always on the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt mens rea, the guilty mind, or the intention of the accused to commit the offence. There are some narrow exceptions in which presumption is invoked. This proposed amendment would set up a presumption with regard to cheques. In the Criminal Code there is a presumption concerning the possession of stolen goods. Few other such presumptions exist in the law. Because a presumption shifts the onus from the Crown to the accused, and that onus is not light, 1 oppose this bill in its present form and hope the Minister of Justice will take steps to look into the matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) for introducing Bill C-230, "an act to amend the Criminal Code (presumption from cheque issued without funds)." The explanatory note to the bill reads:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Criminal Code to provide that the issuance of a cheque returned NSF shall raise a presumption that anything obtained thereby was obtained by false pretence, unless the maker of the cheque satisfies the debt within a period of thirty days after being notified that the cheque was dishonoured.
The explanatory note quotes the wording of subsection 320(4) of the Criminal Code, which at present reads as follows:
... Where, in proceedings under paragraph (l)(a), it is shown that anything was obtained by the accused by means of a cheque that, when presented for payment within a reasonable time, was dishonoured on the ground that no funds or insufficient funds were on deposit to the credit of the accused in the bank or other institution on which the cheque was drawn, it shall be presumed to have been obtained by a false pretence, unless the court is satisfied by evidence that when the accused issued the cheque he had reasonable grounds to believe that it would be honoured if presented for payment within a reasonable time after it was issued.
According to this provision there is a presumption of guilt, that is to say, the onus is upon the accused to provide proof that at the time he wrote the cheque he sincerely believed he had sufficient funds in his bank account to cover the amount.
May 27, 1977

It would appear that this is in direct violation of the time-honoured presumption of innocence until guilt is proven.
I realize that we are dealing with a very complex issue here. Proving the intent to defraud is a very slippery matter. Intent is not necessarily a component of the proof of guilt. In this case unless someone actually said "I am going to write an NSF cheque" it would be extremely difficult to have actual, hard evidence. Canadian law is not alone in its demand that intent be proven. In England, for example, the law requires proof that the accused person acted dishonestly. Similarly, Australian law demands proof of the intent to defraud, although in this country the burden of proof lies with the prosecution rather than with the defendant to disprove. In the states of California, Maine, Michigan and New York a person can be found guilty of passing a bad cheque if, and only if, actual intent to defraud the victim can be found.
The solution to the acquisition of evidence proving the intentional writing of an NSF cheque would be some type of application of a test of intent. Bill C-230 provides the means for that test. If after 30 days a cheque was not honoured it could be assumed that intent had been proven by non-payment.
This bill is designed to rectify a deficiency in the current law governing commercial transactions. As we all know, the law dealing with bad cheques is plain in its intent, but difficult at best and impossible at worst to enforce. The law allows the accused to use as his defence the claim that when he issued the cheque he had reasonable grounds to believe it would be honoured if presented for payment within a reasonable time after it was issued. This is fine as far as it goes.
I am sure that many of us have inadvertently and innocently written an NSF cheque at one time or another. The present law rightly recognizes the possibility of making a legitimate error. But the law should also recognize the rights of those to whom the cheque is issued. I believe that this bill helps to right the balance between the cheque issuer and the cheque recipient, for we should recognize that the Criminal Code, as it stands, has opened not a crack but a superhighway through the law as it now exists. By failing to provide for restitution to the victim, it seems to me the law has missed the point.
I think the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) know how reluctant police are to lay charges in these cases, and how reluctant justices of the peace, magistrates, or provincial judges, as the case may be, are to deal with them. It is often the case, as the police, magistrates or provincial judges know, that a charge is laid in an attempt to use the criminal courts as a collection agency. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton has merit, namely, that part of the sentence should call for the restitution of the amount of money for which the cheque is issued.
The benefits of this change in the law will affect us all. The cost of bad cheques has been twofold. It has been added on to the prices the rest of us pay. It also increases the storekeeper's reluctance to accept a cheque, any cheque, as a means of payment. How many of us have been in stores recently and
Criminal Code
seen the increasingly familiar "We do not accept cheques" sign? How embarrassingly familiar is the current ad for one of the credit card syndicates that asks, "Will that be cash, or-?" By lessening the risk to the merchant in accepting a cheque and decreasing the proportion of bad cheques, the mark-up on merchandise may be lowered. At least some of the merchant's reluctance to accept a cheque will be reduced.
Lest my colleagues think I am exaggerating, allow me to illustrate my point. A local Ottawa merchant stated that in 1976 his company lost $100,000 owing to bad cheques. A clothing chain store controller reported that his chain no longer accepted cheques as a form of payment. They will accept cash or credit cards. The reason? One cheque in ten issued to his firm bounced. Some retailers have found that up to 10 per cent of their annual revenues have been wiped out because of bad cheques.
The London Free Press reported in February that one woman was convicted this winter of defrauding 19 merchants of more than $3,500. In fact she passed 53 "bad cheques" totalling $4,925. In sentencing this offender the judge stated:
It is no wonder that law-abiding citizens encounter problems when they try to write a cheque. The stores have been taken already by too many persons like yourself.
I received, this February, a letter from a woman whose husband has been a victim of NSF cheques and I would like to take the liberty of reading it.
Dear Sir:
May I say how much we appreciate your bringing the NSF cheque issue to light. My husband is a small businessman-he has a franchise for selling snap-on tools. He accepts cheques from customers in good faith, then, when a cheque "bounces", there is not a thing we can do about it. I can telephone day after day, and where they have moved to another location this costs us extra for long distance calls, but to no avail. We offer to take the tools back, but don't get too far on this very often as they need the tools for their line of work. We have paid for lawyers' letters, but to the type of person that writes NSF cheques a lawyer's letter doesn't mean a thing. They know there is no penalty so they can go on writing cheques. Nobody can prove that they didn't know the money was not in the bank.
As with most other small business people, we have to pay for the tools within the week. My husband works many more hours than the fellow who writes the NSF cheques.
It would be a fair ruling, that if the cheques are not honoured within 30 days, goods should be returned. That is a fair enough bill and should be passed.
Thank you for supporting the bill.
The benefits of the hon. member's bill to the shopkeeper are obvious. By attaching the international dishonouring of a cheque to the Criminal Code, the merchant will have recourse to the Crown attorney. This is particularly important, for this bill is aimed at helping the retailer who has lost $200 or less in the transaction. Often the cost of implementing private proceedings outweighs the value of the Items lost. If my hon. colleagues see fit to approve this amendment the merchant will no longer have to bear the burden of instituting proceedings himself, the cost of which must be measured not only in dollars, but in time and energy spent before the legalities begin. The retailer would have a specific time frame to operate within; after 30 days, legal action could be taken.

The unfortunate person who, through miscalculation, has written an NSF cheque would not be subject to harassment by the retailer or a collection agency for both would know that there was a 30 day limit for repayment. The innocent offender could make quick restitution, and the shopkeeper be assured that the law was on his side after the 30 day limit had expired.
Obviously the honest customer will also benefit. He will be less suspect when he wants to write a cheque for merchandise. He will likely also benefit through reduced price tags.
The 30 day time limit will allow the police and the judiciary to determine real intent to defraud. If restitution has not been made within that time, it is likely that it will not be made. In Ottawa alone, last year the police recorded that in 1,372 cases of cheques and credit card fraud, involving $420,000 worth of goods, only 128 arrests were made. Guilt through intent is difficult to establish. While the 30 day limit is not the only measure that can be taken, it would allow an easier determination of guilt by the police and would consequently provide for stricter enforcement of the anti-fraud laws.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I do not believe that this amendment is the ultimate solution. Certainly some less scrupulous individual is likely to make use of the 30 day grace period to purchase items by cheque knowing full well that there is no money in his account, but counting on his U.I.C., pension, family allowance, or income tax return cheque to come before the expiry date. However, I also believe these incidents would be few and far between and that the benefits of this amendment will outweigh this drawback, which could, incidentally, be overcome by the simple imposition of a percentage charge, as is done on overdue accounts.
1 would therefore urge my colleagues to support this bill of the hon. member for London East in his efforts to correct the injustices suffered by merchants and honest cheque writers alike.

If the hon. member is placing a value on my speech I should like to have it in cash rather than by cheque. I know what side of the House he sits on.
I should like to reiterate a couple of thoughts which have already been put forward this afternoon. The first is that the bill has the effect of giving 30 days' grace, or licence. I know that the hon. member who has just taken his seat made a reference to' this. He said that innocent offenders would have 30 days in which to make restitution. But if the innocent can do this, so can those who are not so innocent. It is unlikely that 100 per cent of our population is composed of innocent individuals with the same high motives as the supporters of this measure. And there is no doubt that people without high motives would be in a position to abuse the privilege or loopholes which it provides.
There is another part of the bill to which 1 take exception. If the 30 day requirement is not met, an offence automatically becomes a criminal one.
